10|ENZAMET Trial is provided in the Supple-

17|BACKGROUND
18|Enzalutamide, an androgen-receptor inhibitor, has been associated with improved
19|overall survival in men with castration-resistant prostate cancer. It is not known
20|whether adding enzalutamide to testosterone suppression, with or without early
21|docetaxel, will improve survival in men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
22|tate cancer.
23|METHODS
24|In this open-label, randomized, phase 3 trial, we assigned patients to receive tes-
25|tosterone suppression plus either open-label enzalutamide or a standard nonsteroidal
26|antiandrogen therapy (standard-care group). The primary end point was overall
27|survival. Secondary end points included progression-free survival as determined by
28|the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level, clinical progression-free survival, and
29|adverse events.
30|RESULTS
31|A total of 1125 men underwent randomization; the median follow-up was 34 months.
32|There were 102 deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths in the standard-
33|care group (hazard ratio, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.86; P = 0.002).
34|Kaplan-Meier estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80% (based on 94 events)
35|in the enzalutamide group and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-care group.
36|Better results with enzalutamide were also seen in PSA progression-free survival (174
37|and 333 events, respectively; hazard ratio, 0.39; P<0.001) and in clinical progression-
38|free survival (167 and 320 events, respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; P<0.001). Treat-
39|ment discontinuation due to adverse events was more frequent in the enzalutamide
40|group than in the standard-care group (33 events and 14 events, respectively). Fa-
41|tigue was more common in the enzalutamide group; seizures occurred in 7 patients
42|in the enzalutamide group (1%) and in no patients in the standard-care group.
43|CONCLUSIONS
44|Enzalutamide was associated with significantly longer progression-free and overall
45|survival than standard care in men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer
46|receiving testosterone suppression. The enzalutamide group had a higher incidence of
47|seizures and other toxic effects, especially among those treated with early docetax-
48|el. (Funded by Astellas Scientific and Medical Affairs and others; ENZAMET
49|(ANZUP 1304) ANZCTR number, ACTRN12614000110684; ClinicalTrials.gov num-
50|ber, NCT02446405; and EU Clinical Trials Register number, 2014-003190-42.)

4|S
5|everal randomized trials have es-
6|tablished the benefits of adding docetaxel
7|or abiraterone to testosterone suppression
8|in men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
9|tate cancer.1-10 The survival benefits associated
10|with docetaxel early in the course of treatment,
11|particularly in men with high-volume metastatic
12|disease,7 are substantially larger than the survival
13|benefits associated with using docetaxel later af-
14|ter castration resistance has developed.11-13 The
15|addition of abiraterone to testosterone suppression
16|also improved overall survival in hormone-sensi-
17|tive prostate cancer, regardless of the burden of
18|metastatic disease.9,10 A recent post hoc compari-
19|son indicated that men who were given abiraterone
20|or docetaxel early in the course of treatment had
21|similar outcomes with respect to overall survival.14
22|Enzalutamide is an orally administered, small-
23|molecule inhibitor of the androgen receptor that
24|is designed to overcome acquired resistance to
25|first-generation nonsteroidal antiandrogens, in-
26|cluding bicalutamide, nilutamide, and flutamide.
27|Previous trials have shown that enzalutamide
28|improved overall survival in castration-resistant
29|prostate cancer, regardless of whether it was used
30|before or after docetaxel chemotherapy.15,16
31|We hypothesized that adding enzalutamide to
32|first-line therapy would delay the emergence of
33|castration resistance and thereby improve overall
34|survival. In the ENZAMET (Enzalutamide in First
35|Line Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Metastatic
36|Prostate Cancer) trial, our aim was to determine
37|the effects of adding enzalutamide to first-line
38|treatment that included testosterone suppression
39|with or without early docetaxel.
40|Methods
41|Trial Design
42|The primary objective of this multinational, open-
43|label, randomized, phase 3 trial was to determine
44|the effects of early enzalutamide treatment on
45|overall survival in men with metastatic, hormone-
46|sensitive prostate cancer. Secondary objectives
47|were to determine the effects on progression-free
48|survival as determined by the prostate-specific
49|antigen (PSA) level, clinical progression-free sur-
50|vival (based on imaging, symptoms, signs, or
51|changes in therapy), and adverse events. Effects
52|on health-related quality of life, resource use, and
53|incremental cost-effectiveness will be reported
54|separately.
55|Patients and Treatment
56|Eligible patients had prostatic adenocarcinoma
57|with metastases on computed tomography (CT),
58|bone scanning with technetium-99, or both and
59|a score of 2 or less on the Eastern Cooperative
60|Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status scale,
61|which ranges from 0 (no disability) to 5 (death).
62|Testosterone suppression was initiated up to 12
63|weeks before randomization. Previous adjuvant
64|testosterone suppression for up to 24 months was
65|allowed if the treatment had been completed at
66|least 12 months earlier. The trial protocol and
67|Supplementary Appendix are available with the
68|full text of this article at NEJM.org.
69|Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a
70|1:1 ratio to receive enzalutamide (at a dose of
71|160 mg daily) or a standard nonsteroidal antian-
72|drogen drug (bicalutamide, nilutamide, or flu-
73|tamide) (standard-care group) until the occur-
74|rence of clinical disease progression or prohibitive
75|toxic effects. In the two groups, background ther-
76|apy included continuous testosterone suppression.
77|After the enrollment of 88 patients (mainly from
78|Australia and New Zealand), the early adminis-
79|tration of docetaxel with testosterone suppression
80|was permitted in protocol version 2 (as revised on
81|November 2014) as a stratification factor before
82|randomization, according to evidence showing
83|improved survival with this approach.1 The deci-
84|sion to initiate early treatment with docetaxel was
85|left up to the individual patients and their physi-
86|cians. If docetaxel was administered, the regimen
87|consisted of 75 mg per square meter of body-
88|surface area, without prednisone or prednisolone,
89|given every 3 weeks for a maximum of six cycles.
90|Up to two cycles of docetaxel were permitted be-
91|fore randomization.
92|The central randomization system implement-
93|ed minimization with a random component. Ran-
94|domization was stratified according to the volume
95|of disease (high [defined as the presence of vis-
96|ceral metastases or at least four bone lesions with
97|at least one lesion located beyond the vertebral
98|bodies and pelvis] or low), planned use of early
99|docetaxel (yes or no), planned use of bone anti-
100|resorptive therapy (yes or no), the score on the
101|Adult Comorbidity Evaluation 27 (ACE-27)17 (with

6|tions]), and trial site.
7|Trial Oversight
8|The trial was led by the Australian and New
9|Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
10|Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
11|Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
12|Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
13|sponsorship and coordination was performed by
14|Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
15|Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
16|Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
17|in the United States. The trial was designed by the
18|ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
19|analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
20|The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
21|ing of the manuscript.
22|Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
23|financial support for trial conduct; representa-
24|tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
25|tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
26|volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
27|accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
28|Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
29|drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
30|were accessed according to local standard prac-
31|tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
32|completeness of the reported data and for the
33|fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
34|An independent data and safety monitoring
35|committee reviewed the progress and results of
36|the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
37|with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
38|guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
39|protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
40|proved as required at each participating institu-
41|tion. All the patients provided written informed
42|consent.
43|End Points
44|The primary end point of overall survival was
45|measured as the interval from randomization to
46|death from any cause or to the date at which the
47|patient was last known to be alive. The second-
48|ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
49|was measured as the interval from randomiza-
50|tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
51|cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
52|Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
53|in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
54|and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
55|sion, death from any cause, or the last known
56|date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
57|secondary end point of clinical progression was
58|defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
59|gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
60|Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
61|the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
62|mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
63|development of symptoms attributable to cancer
64|progression; or the initiation of another antican-
65|cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
66|means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
67|mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
68|gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
69|images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
70|verse events were graded according to the Na-
71|tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
72|Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
73|verse-event data were collected during the treat-
74|ment period, with a final safety assessment
75|performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
76|the trial regimen.
77|Statistical Analysis
78|We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
79|tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
80|of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
81|death in the enzalutamide group than in the
82|standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
83|two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
84|culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
85|65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
86|two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
87|with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
88|cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
89|an interim analysis of overall survival after the
90|occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
91|deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
92|spending function. Protocol version 3, which
93|was written after external evidence became
94|available for improved overall survival with early
95|abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
96|of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
97|and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
98|trial executive committee made these decisions
99|without any knowledge of outcomes in each
100|treatment group.

18|The first interim analysis of the primary end
19|point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
20|occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
21|independent data and safety monitoring com-
22|mittee recommended that the unblinded results
23|be provided to the trial executive committee so
24|that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
25|mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
26|rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
27|esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
28|The results that are reported here include 10
29|additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
30|view to ascertain the survival status of all the
31|patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
32|follow-up of 34 months.
33|At the time of this analysis, there were 102
34|deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
35|in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
36|death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
37|0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
38|fected by adjustments for geographical region,
39|volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
40|ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
41|conditions. The median survival time was not yet
42|estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
43|estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
44|(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
45|and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
46|care group.
47|Progression-free Survival
48|The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
49|free survival and clinical progression-free survival
50|were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
51|PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
52|events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
53|in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
54|survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
55|hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
56|(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
57|there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
58|and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
59|of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
60|respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
61|0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
62|the between-group difference in PSA progres-
63|sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
64|survival remained highly significant after adjust-
65|ment for multiple comparisons.
66|Subgroup Analyses
67|The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
68|were smaller among the patients in the stratified
69|subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
70|therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
71|high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
72|Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
73|multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
74|of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
75|0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
76|el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
77|resorptive therapy.
78|We anticipated that the smaller number of
79|deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
80|analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
81|in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
82|progression-free survival would also be per-
83|formed to take advantage of the larger number
84|of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
85|fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
86|free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
87|groups, including those with early docetaxel
88|treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
89|tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
90|on clinical progression-free survival according to
91|the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
92|el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
93|of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
94|disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
95|ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
96|treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
97|significant after adjustment for multiple com-
98|parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
99|tary Appendix).
100|Subsequent Anticancer Therapies
101|Treatment after progression was initiated at the
102|discretion of the patients and their physicians.

7|with the higher incidence of clinical progression
8|in the standard-care group. Among the patients

10|in the enzalutamide group and 271 of 320 (85%)
11|in the standard-care group received one or more
12|subsequent life-prolonging therapies (Table S4
13|in the Supplementary Appendix).
14|Treatment Duration
15|At 3 years, the percentage of patients who were
16|still receiving a trial regimen was 62% in the
17|enzalutamide group and 34% in the standard-care

4|The effect of enzalutamide on overall survival
5|appeared to be smaller in the subgroup with
6|early docetaxel treatment. However, this trial was
7|neither designed nor powered to reliably analyze
8|the results in this subgroup. The effects of enzalu-
9|tamide on clinical progression-free survival, an
10|earlier end point with considerably more events
11|and consequently greater statistical reliability,
12|remained substantial regardless of early docetax-
13|el treatment. This finding indicates that longer
14|follow-up is needed to determine the effects of
15|enzalutamide on overall survival beyond 3 years
16|in those with early docetaxel treatment. Our cur-
17|rent data support the claim that early enzalu-
18|tamide prolongs survival within 3 years in the
19|entire trial population but provide limited sup-
20|port that it prolongs overall survival within 3 years
21|in patients who received early docetaxel treatment.
22|The main limitations of this trial are conse-
23|quences of the detection of evidence of benefit at
24|the first planned interim analysis. This early analy-
25|sis may have overestimated the eventual treatment
26|benefit.20 There was no central review of actual
27|imaging, but this factor would have no effect on
28|the rate of death, the primary end point. The me-
29|dian follow-up of 34 months is sufficient to pro-
30|vide evidence about the effects within this interval
31|but not beyond it. The sample size and number
32|of events allow for strong conclusions about the
33|effects of enzalutamide on survival in the entire
34|trial population and the effects on progression-
35|free survival in some subgroups; however, we
36|cannot determine the effects on overall survival
37|in any of the prespecified subgroups.
38|In conclusion, in men with metastatic hor-
39|mone-sensitive prostate cancer receiving testos-
40|terone suppression, the addition of enzalutamide
41|resulted in longer overall survival, PSA progres-
42|sion-free survival, and clinical progression-free
43|survival within 3 years than the use of standard
44|nonsteroidal antiandrogen therapy. However,
45|enzalutamide was associated with some additional
46|toxic effects, including fatigue and a small risk of
47|seizures. Among the patients who also received
48|early docetaxel treatment, the addition of enzalu-
49|tamide was associated with additional toxic ef-
50|fects and longer progression-free survival but not
51|longer overall survival.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.

Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
Clinical progression free survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to the
date of first clinical evidence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first,
or the date of last known follow-up without clinical progression (at which point the observation is
censored). The censoring date will be the latest of the following: the date of the patient's last
assessment during the 'on treatment' phase where clinical progression status is recorded as 'no';
and, the maximum date the patient is last known not to have progressed collected during the 'post-
treatment follow-up' phase. Clinical progression is defined by progression on imaging, development
of symptoms attributable to cancer progression, or initiation of other anticancer treatment for
prostate cancer.

S
everal randomized trials have es-
tablished the benefits of adding docetaxel
or abiraterone to testosterone suppression
in men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
tate cancer.1-10 The survival benefits associated
with docetaxel early in the course of treatment,
particularly in men with high-volume metastatic
disease,7 are substantially larger than the survival
benefits associated with using docetaxel later af-
ter castration resistance has developed.11-13 The
addition of abiraterone to testosterone suppression
also improved overall survival in hormone-sensi-
tive prostate cancer, regardless of the burden of
metastatic disease.9,10 A recent post hoc compari-
son indicated that men who were given abiraterone
or docetaxel early in the course of treatment had
similar outcomes with respect to overall survival.14
Enzalutamide is an orally administered, small-
molecule inhibitor of the androgen receptor that
is designed to overcome acquired resistance to
first-generation nonsteroidal antiandrogens, in-
cluding bicalutamide, nilutamide, and flutamide.
Previous trials have shown that enzalutamide
improved overall survival in castration-resistant
prostate cancer, regardless of whether it was used
before or after docetaxel chemotherapy.15,16
We hypothesized that adding enzalutamide to
first-line therapy would delay the emergence of
castration resistance and thereby improve overall
survival. In the ENZAMET (Enzalutamide in First
Line Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Metastatic
Prostate Cancer) trial, our aim was to determine
the effects of adding enzalutamide to first-line
treatment that included testosterone suppression
with or without early docetaxel.
Methods
Trial Design
The primary objective of this multinational, open-
label, randomized, phase 3 trial was to determine
the effects of early enzalutamide treatment on
overall survival in men with metastatic, hormone-
sensitive prostate cancer. Secondary objectives
were to determine the effects on progression-free

Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

questions.bias_construct: Whether context-caused protocol-inconsistent deviations were balanced between intervention groups.
considerations: Balance refers to the deviations identified in 2.3 and their potential effect, not to baseline group sizes.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the identified deviations were balanced between groups; answer no or probably no when they were not balanced.
evidence_needed: Group-specific counts or descriptions of the identified deviations and their comparability between intervention groups.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when balance of the identified deviations cannot be determined.
questions.official_guidance: Changes from assigned intervention that are inconsistent with the trial protocol and arose because of the trial context are more likely to impact on intervention effect estimate if they are not balanced between the intervention groups.

answer_anchors.text: An ITT or appropriate modified ITT analysis estimated assignment effect.
A naive per-protocol, as-treated, or inappropriate post-randomization exclusion analysis was used.

questions.bias_construct: Whether an appropriate analysis estimated the effect of assignment to intervention. Compare randomized assignment with the actual analysis population, grouping, reassignment, and exclusions, including their reasons; an ITT, modified ITT, or as-treated label alone does not establish this.
considerations: The question is about effect of assignment, so grouping must follow randomized assignment.
Assess what the analysis actually did, not the label attached to it: ITT/mITT/as-treated terminology is a description to verify against assignment, grouping, and exclusions.

Never-treated participants are not automatically participants with no adverse event or unavailable outcome. Recover the documented eligibility, outcome availability, and exclusion reason before judging the approved assignment-effect estimand.

A post-randomization exclusion of an eligible participant remains an analysis concern whether it happened before the endpoint was measured or after an outcome value was recorded. Record that timing separately: an outcome not collected may also matter to D3, while an observed value omitted from the assignment analysis is not thereby missing outcome data. Judge 2.7 from the excluded participants, reasons, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance for this Result.
questions.decision_rule: Consider ITT and modified ITT excluding participants with missing outcome data appropriate. Consider naive per-protocol, as-treated, and post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants inappropriate; post-randomization exclusion of ineligible participants may be appropriate when eligibility could not have been influenced by assignment.
evidence_needed: The actual analysis population and grouping rule: who was assigned, who was analysed in each group, who was excluded or reassigned after randomization, and why.
invalid_shortcuts: an ITT label without its population
a per-protocol label without the analysis population
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an incomplete analysis description alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment about appropriateness.
questions.official_guidance: Both intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses and modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate. Both naïve ‘per-protocol’ analyses and ‘as treated’ analyses should be considered inappropriate. Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate.

questions.bias_construct: Whether failure to analyse participants in their randomized group could substantially affect the result.
considerations: This is conditional on an inappropriate or uncertain analysis in 2.6.
Assess potential impact only after deciding whether 2.6 was appropriate; a small or balanced exclusion can have low impact without making an inappropriate analysis appropriate.

Use facts about this endpoint and the excluded participants. Exclusion before outcome ascertainment may also leave outcome data missing; exclusion after ascertainment may omit observed values from the analysis. Neither timing alone settles the possible effect on the estimate.
questions.decision_rule: Assess whether the number analysed in the wrong group or excluded was sufficient for substantial impact. There is no precise percentage rule: fewer than 5% may still matter for rare outcomes or exclusions strongly related to prognostic factors.
evidence_needed: Counts and reasons for participants analysed in the wrong group or excluded, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance of exclusions.

questions.official_guidance: This question addresses whether the number of participants who were analysed in the wrong intervention group, or excluded from the analysis, was sufficient that there could have been a substantial impact on the result. It is not possible to specify a precise rule: there may be potential for substantial impact even if fewer than 5% of participants were analysed in the wrong group or excluded, if the outcome is rare or if exclusions are strongly related to prognostic factors.

Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
Clinical progression free survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to the
date of first clinical evidence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first,
or the date of last known follow-up without clinical progression (at which point the observation is
censored). The censoring date will be the latest of the following: the date of the patient's last
assessment during the 'on treatment' phase where clinical progression status is recorded as 'no';
and, the maximum date the patient is last known not to have progressed collected during the 'post-
treatment follow-up' phase. Clinical progression is defined by progression on imaging, development
of symptoms attributable to cancer progression, or initiation of other anticancer treatment for
prostate cancer.

everal randomized trials have es-
tablished the benefits of adding docetaxel
or abiraterone to testosterone suppression
in men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
tate cancer.1-10 The survival benefits associated
with docetaxel early in the course of treatment,
particularly in men with high-volume metastatic
disease,7 are substantially larger than the survival
benefits associated with using docetaxel later af-
ter castration resistance has developed.11-13 The
addition of abiraterone to testosterone suppression
also improved overall survival in hormone-sensi-
tive prostate cancer, regardless of the burden of
metastatic disease.9,10 A recent post hoc compari-
son indicated that men who were given abiraterone
or docetaxel early in the course of treatment had
similar outcomes with respect to overall survival.14
Enzalutamide is an orally administered, small-
molecule inhibitor of the androgen receptor that
is designed to overcome acquired resistance to
first-generation nonsteroidal antiandrogens, in-
cluding bicalutamide, nilutamide, and flutamide.
Previous trials have shown that enzalutamide
improved overall survival in castration-resistant
prostate cancer, regardless of whether it was used
before or after docetaxel chemotherapy.15,16
We hypothesized that adding enzalutamide to
first-line therapy would delay the emergence of
castration resistance and thereby improve overall
survival. In the ENZAMET (Enzalutamide in First
Line Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Metastatic
Prostate Cancer) trial, our aim was to determine
the effects of adding enzalutamide to first-line
treatment that included testosterone suppression
with or without early docetaxel.
Methods
Trial Design
The primary objective of this multinational, open-
label, randomized, phase 3 trial was to determine
the effects of early enzalutamide treatment on
overall survival in men with metastatic, hormone-
sensitive prostate cancer. Secondary objectives
were to determine the effects on progression-free
survival as determined by the prostate-specific
antigen (PSA) level, clinical progression-free sur-
vival (based on imaging, symptoms, signs, or
changes in therapy), and adverse events. Effects
on health-related quality of life, resource use, and
incremental cost-effectiveness will be reported
separately.
Patients and Treatment
Eligible patients had prostatic adenocarcinoma
with metastases on computed tomography (CT),
bone scanning with technetium-99, or both and
a score of 2 or less on the Eastern Cooperative
Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status scale,
which ranges from 0 (no disability) to 5 (death).
Testosterone suppression was initiated up to 12
weeks before randomization. Previous adjuvant
testosterone suppression for up to 24 months was
allowed if the treatment had been completed at
least 12 months earlier. The trial protocol and
Supplementary Appendix are available with the
full text of this article at NEJM.org.
Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a
1:1 ratio to receive enzalutamide (at a dose of
160 mg daily) or a standard nonsteroidal antian-
drogen drug (bicalutamide, nilutamide, or flu-
tamide) (standard-care group) until the occur-
rence of clinical disease progression or prohibitive
toxic effects. In the two groups, background ther-
apy included continuous testosterone suppression.
After the enrollment of 88 patients (mainly from
Australia and New Zealand), the early adminis-
tration of docetaxel with testosterone suppression
was permitted in protocol version 2 (as revised on
November 2014) as a stratification factor before
randomization, according to evidence showing
improved survival with this approach.1 The deci-
sion to initiate early treatment with docetaxel was
left up to the individual patients and their physi-
cians. If docetaxel was administered, the regimen
consisted of 75 mg per square meter of body-
surface area, without prednisone or prednisolone,
given every 3 weeks for a maximum of six cycles.
Up to two cycles of docetaxel were permitted be-
fore randomization.
The central randomization system implement-
ed minimization with a random component. Ran-
domization was stratified according to the volume
of disease (high [defined as the presence of vis-
ceral metastases or at least four bone lesions with
at least one lesion located beyond the vertebral
bodies and pelvis] or low), planned use of early
docetaxel (yes or no), planned use of bone anti-

hormonal therapies (enzalutamide, abiraterone), cytotoxic therapy and vaccine therapy for

This protocol is based on the hypothesis that earlier use of a therapy shown to be effective in
the more advanced state of castration resistant prostate cancer will prevent or delay the
emergence of castration resistant disease and will prolong overall survival. As such this protocol
aims to determine whether the potent second generation androgen receptor inhibitor,
enzalutamide can enhance the ability of androgen suppression to increase the longevity of men
commencing androgen suppression for newly metastatic prostate cancer.

The current treatment for patients commencing hormonal therapy for metastatic prostate cancer
is androgen suppression either by LHRH analogue therapy or orchidectomy as monotherapy or
in combination with an anti-androgen, also known as combined androgen deprivation therapy.
Survival varies depending on the extent of disease at commencement of therapy. With the
advent of the PSA test many patients are commenced on hormonal therapy at a very early
stage (biochemical recurrence) and subjected to the long-term effects of androgen deprivation
including osteoporosis. However, if patients with an asymptomatic rising PSA after definitive
local therapy are observed until they develop overt metastatic disease (i.e. evident by imaging
techniques), the median time from PSA relapse to clinical progression is approximately 8 years.

answers.justification: The report identifies ENZAMET as an open-label randomized trial and describes treatment assignments. Participants were aware of their assigned intervention.
The report describes the trial as open label, and the treating clinicians and investigators delivered the assigned treatments. They were aware of assignment.

The protocol allows treatment discontinuation for clinical progression, toxicity, investigator judgment, participant choice, and specified compliance issues, and requires follow-up after stopping treatment. The report describes discontinuations and subsequent treatment following progression. I found no evidence that the trial context caused a protocol-inconsistent change; the reported changes fit the protocol's treatment course or ordinary post-progression care.
unknowns: The article does not give a complete group-specific account of every treatment deviation or its cause.

questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Neutral paired control: complete ascertainment and an analysis denominator with unresolved ascertainment differ only in the availability premise; administrative censoring and worsening-related follow-up loss differ only in the missingness mechanism.

Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
coexisting conditions rated as 0 [none] or 1 [mild]
vs. 2 [moderate] or 3 [severe or multiple condi-
tions]), and trial site.
Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
Clinical progression free survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to the
date of first clinical evidence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first,
or the date of last known follow-up without clinical progression (at which point the observation is
censored). The censoring date will be the latest of the following: the date of the patient's last
assessment during the 'on treatment' phase where clinical progression status is recorded as 'no';
and, the maximum date the patient is last known not to have progressed collected during the 'post-
treatment follow-up' phase. Clinical progression is defined by progression on imaging, development
of symptoms attributable to cancer progression, or initiation of other anticancer treatment for
prostate cancer.

everal randomized trials have es-
tablished the benefits of adding docetaxel
or abiraterone to testosterone suppression
in men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
tate cancer.1-10 The survival benefits associated
with docetaxel early in the course of treatment,
particularly in men with high-volume metastatic
disease,7 are substantially larger than the survival
benefits associated with using docetaxel later af-
ter castration resistance has developed.11-13 The
addition of abiraterone to testosterone suppression
also improved overall survival in hormone-sensi-
tive prostate cancer, regardless of the burden of
metastatic disease.9,10 A recent post hoc compari-
son indicated that men who were given abiraterone
or docetaxel early in the course of treatment had
similar outcomes with respect to overall survival.14
Enzalutamide is an orally administered, small-
molecule inhibitor of the androgen receptor that
is designed to overcome acquired resistance to
first-generation nonsteroidal antiandrogens, in-
cluding bicalutamide, nilutamide, and flutamide.
Previous trials have shown that enzalutamide
improved overall survival in castration-resistant
prostate cancer, regardless of whether it was used
before or after docetaxel chemotherapy.15,16
We hypothesized that adding enzalutamide to
first-line therapy would delay the emergence of
castration resistance and thereby improve overall
survival. In the ENZAMET (Enzalutamide in First
Line Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Metastatic
Prostate Cancer) trial, our aim was to determine
the effects of adding enzalutamide to first-line
treatment that included testosterone suppression
with or without early docetaxel.
Methods
Trial Design
The primary objective of this multinational, open-
label, randomized, phase 3 trial was to determine
the effects of early enzalutamide treatment on
overall survival in men with metastatic, hormone-
sensitive prostate cancer. Secondary objectives
were to determine the effects on progression-free
survival as determined by the prostate-specific
antigen (PSA) level, clinical progression-free sur-
vival (based on imaging, symptoms, signs, or
changes in therapy), and adverse events. Effects
on health-related quality of life, resource use, and
incremental cost-effectiveness will be reported
separately.
Patients and Treatment
Eligible patients had prostatic adenocarcinoma
with metastases on computed tomography (CT),
bone scanning with technetium-99, or both and
a score of 2 or less on the Eastern Cooperative
Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status scale,
which ranges from 0 (no disability) to 5 (death).
Testosterone suppression was initiated up to 12
weeks before randomization. Previous adjuvant
testosterone suppression for up to 24 months was
allowed if the treatment had been completed at
least 12 months earlier. The trial protocol and
Supplementary Appendix are available with the
full text of this article at NEJM.org.
Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a
1:1 ratio to receive enzalutamide (at a dose of
160 mg daily) or a standard nonsteroidal antian-
drogen drug (bicalutamide, nilutamide, or flu-
tamide) (standard-care group) until the occur-
rence of clinical disease progression or prohibitive
toxic effects. In the two groups, background ther-
apy included continuous testosterone suppression.
After the enrollment of 88 patients (mainly from
Australia and New Zealand), the early adminis-
tration of docetaxel with testosterone suppression
was permitted in protocol version 2 (as revised on
November 2014) as a stratification factor before
randomization, according to evidence showing
improved survival with this approach.1 The deci-
sion to initiate early treatment with docetaxel was
left up to the individual patients and their physi-
cians. If docetaxel was administered, the regimen
consisted of 75 mg per square meter of body-
surface area, without prednisone or prednisolone,
given every 3 weeks for a maximum of six cycles.
Up to two cycles of docetaxel were permitted be-
fore randomization.
The central randomization system implement-

domization was stratified according to the volume

ceral metastases or at least four bone lesions with

bodies and pelvis] or low), planned use of early

answers.justification: The article reports efficacy analysis of all 1,125 randomized participants and states that relevant event-free follow-up was included as censored observations. It separately identifies only 14 patients lost to follow-up or withdrawing consent, and the supplement gives their arm-specific counts (4 in enzalutamide; 10 in NSAA) while showing both full randomized groups in the ITT analyses. This is a small fraction of the randomized population and supports availability for nearly all participants for the reported time-to-event analysis.
unknowns: The report does not give endpoint-specific censoring times for each of the 14 patients or a complete count of administrative censoring at the data cutoff.

counterevidence.implication: Fourteen patients were lost to follow-up or withdrew consent; the supplement reports median survival follow-up of 7.2 months for the four enzalutamide withdrawals and 7.7 months for the ten NSAA patients who withdrew or were lost, including two immediate post-randomization withdrawals. These early censorings could leave their later progression status unknown, although their number is small and their available times were included in the analysis.

questions.wording: Was the method of measuring the outcome inappropriate?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if the method of measuring the outcome is inappropriate, for example because it is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the measurement instrument has been demonstrated to have poor validity.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate for the outcome, including validity and sensitivity to plausible intervention effects.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. Validity and sensitivity are distinct from detection opportunity, assessor identity or awareness, and whether knowledge influenced assessment. Do not assess whether choosing the outcome itself was sensible.
evidence_needed: The measurement method's sensitivity to plausible effects and evidence of instrument validity for this outcome.

For a mixed objective and subjective composite, inspect each component that can determine the approved event; objective components do not establish validity or influence conclusions for a subjective component.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when appropriateness of the measurement method cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The measurement method is unsuitable, insensitive, or poorly valid for this outcome.
The measurement method is appropriate for this outcome.

considerations: For pre-specified outcomes the answer will usually be no or probably no.

Measurement susceptibility concerns whether the method can validly and sensitively measure this outcome. It is distinct from assessor awareness, detection opportunity, and whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.

A standardized instrument can still involve judgment in elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment. Preserve component-specific Evidence and uncertainty for mixed objective and subjective components.

Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
coexisting conditions rated as 0 [none] or 1 [mild]
vs. 2 [moderate] or 3 [severe or multiple condi-
tions]), and trial site.
Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

questions.bias_construct: Whether measurement or ascertainment of the outcome could have differed between intervention groups.
considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.

Tie every monitoring difference to the approved event. Extra visits for toxicity monitoring do not establish differential measurement of mortality when death is captured through the same complete registry in both groups; those same visits may change detection of a lab-detected toxicity measured at those visits. State any mortality-specific pathway if one is supported.

For adverse events, compare the actual start and end of the AE observation window, visit schedule, post-treatment follow-up, and ascertainment method with the approved safety window. Treatment duration, median progression-free survival, or a treatment-emergent label alone does not establish when or how adverse events were observed.
Neutral paired control: equal ascertainment schedules and intervention-created additional visits differ only in detection opportunity; do not turn that contrast into an automatic risk label.
questions.decision_rule: Comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points. Consider diagnostic detection bias from passive collection and additional healthcare visits caused by an intervention, but identify the pathway by which a different detection opportunity could change ascertainment before judging its severity.
evidence_needed: Methods, thresholds, timing, and opportunities for outcome ascertainment in each intervention group, plus the pathway connecting any opportunity difference to differential detection.

Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
Clinical progression free survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to the
date of first clinical evidence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first,
or the date of last known follow-up without clinical progression (at which point the observation is

122
The new engl and jour nal of medicine
S
everal randomized trials have es-
tablished the benefits of adding docetaxel
or abiraterone to testosterone suppression
in men with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
tate cancer.1-10 The survival benefits associated
with docetaxel early in the course of treatment,
particularly in men with high-volume metastatic
disease,7 are substantially larger than the survival
benefits associated with using docetaxel later af-
ter castration resistance has developed.11-13 The
addition of abiraterone to testosterone suppression
also improved overall survival in hormone-sensi-
tive prostate cancer, regardless of the burden of
metastatic disease.9,10 A recent post hoc compari-
son indicated that men who were given abiraterone
or docetaxel early in the course of treatment had
similar outcomes with respect to overall survival.14
Enzalutamide is an orally administered, small-
molecule inhibitor of the androgen receptor that
is designed to overcome acquired resistance to
first-generation nonsteroidal antiandrogens, in-
cluding bicalutamide, nilutamide, and flutamide.
Previous trials have shown that enzalutamide
improved overall survival in castration-resistant
prostate cancer, regardless of whether it was used
before or after docetaxel chemotherapy.15,16
We hypothesized that adding enzalutamide to
first-line therapy would delay the emergence of
castration resistance and thereby improve overall
survival. In the ENZAMET (Enzalutamide in First
Line Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Metastatic
Prostate Cancer) trial, our aim was to determine
the effects of adding enzalutamide to first-line
treatment that included testosterone suppression
with or without early docetaxel.
Methods
Trial Design
The primary objective of this multinational, open-
label, randomized, phase 3 trial was to determine
the effects of early enzalutamide treatment on
overall survival in men with metastatic, hormone-
sensitive prostate cancer. Secondary objectives
were to determine the effects on progression-free
survival as determined by the prostate-specific
antigen (PSA) level, clinical progression-free sur-
vival (based on imaging, symptoms, signs, or
changes in therapy), and adverse events. Effects
on health-related quality of life, resource use, and
incremental cost-effectiveness will be reported
separately.

Eligible patients had prostatic adenocarcinoma

bone scanning with technetium-99, or both and
a score of 2 or less on the Eastern Cooperative

which ranges from 0 (no disability) to 5 (death).
Testosterone suppression was initiated up to 12
weeks before randomization. Previous adjuvant
testosterone suppression for up to 24 months was
allowed if the treatment had been completed at
least 12 months earlier. The trial protocol and
Supplementary Appendix are available with the
full text of this article at NEJM.org.
Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a
1:1 ratio to receive enzalutamide (at a dose of
160 mg daily) or a standard nonsteroidal antian-

Overall survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to date of death from any

PSA Progression Free Survival (PSA PFS)
PSA progression free survival (PSA PFS) is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to
the date of first evidence of PSA progression, clinical progression, or death from any cause,
whichever occurs first, or the date of last known follow-up without PSA progression (at which point
the observation is censored).
2.3
Clinical Progression Free Survival (Clinical PFS)
Clinical progression free survival is defined as the interval from the date of randomisation to the
date of first clinical evidence of disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first,
or the date of last known follow-up without clinical progression (at which point the observation is
censored). Clinical progression is defined by progression on imaging, development of symptoms
attributable to cancer progression, or initiation of other anticancer treatment for prostate cancer.

The protocol specifies the clinical PFS definition and a central clinical review of endpoint derivations with programmed endpoint checks. I found no evidence that these measurement methods were unsuitable for clinical progression.

counterevidence.implication: The protocol separately used central clinical review of endpoint derivations with treatment allocation omitted from review outputs, which may reduce awareness for central review; however, clinical progression was first documented by site investigators.

answers.justification: The composite includes symptom attribution and initiation of another anticancer treatment, which involve clinical judgment and treatment decisions. Given open-label conduct, knowledge of assignment could influence these components even though radiographic criteria and central endpoint review provide more objective safeguards.

Although awareness could influence symptom attribution or treatment-initiation decisions, the protocol used central clinical review of endpoint derivations without treatment allocation in the review outputs, and the publication reports no evidence that assignment knowledge changed outcome determinations. This supports that influence was possible but was not shown to be likely.
unknowns: The report does not quantify how often symptoms or treatment-initiation decisions determined the first event, or report an audit of group-specific overrides by central clinical review.

Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
